l: sea of Hashiri-midzu, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Its Deity raises violent waves that prevent Yamato-take’s ship from crossing. Princess Oto-tachibana enters the sea in his place, after which the waves go down.

l: Wohari, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take visits the house of Princess Miyadzu, ancestress of its rulers, and later returns there after his campaigns.

l: Mount Ibuki, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take goes to take its Deity empty-handed. The encounter with the Deity leaves him afflicted by heavy ice-rain and illness.

l: Herb-Quelling-Sabre, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Her Augustness Yamato-hime gives it to Yamato-take before his eastern expedition. He later leaves it in Princess Miyadzu’s house.

l: august bag, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Her Augustness Yamato-hime gives it to Yamato-take with instructions to open it in an emergency. When trapped by fire in Sagamu, he finds a fire-striker inside.

l: august sword, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take uses an august sword to cut through burning herbage in Sagamu. He later finds another august sword that he had left at the single pine-tree on Cape Wotsu and sings about the sword placed at the maiden’s bedside.

l: white dotterel, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: After Yamato-take dies, he turns into a white dotterel eight fathoms long and flies toward the shore. The bird is pursued, buried, and then flies away again toward Shiki.

l: great august mausoleum, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take’s Empresses and children build an august mausoleum and perform songs and lamentations during his interment.

l: August-Mausoleum of the White-Bird, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The mausoleum made at Shiki in the land of Kafuchi is called the August-Mausoleum of the White-Bird after Yamato-take becomes a white dotterel.

l: the savage Deities, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take is commanded to subdue them in the twelve roads of the East and later subdues those of the mountains and rivers.

l: unsubmissive people, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take is sent to pacify unsubmissive people in the twelve roads of the East and in the eastern lands.

l: twelve circuits to the eastward, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The Heavenly Sovereign commands Yamato-take to subdue and pacify their savage Deities and unsubmissive people.

l: Great Deity of Ise, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take enters this deity’s temple and worships the deity’s court before speaking with Yamato-hime.

l: Yamato-take's eastern expedition, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The expedition takes Yamato-take through Wohari, the eastern lands, Sagamu, the sea of Hashiri-midzu, Ashigara, Kahi, Shinanu, and back to Wohari. During it he subdues Deities and people, survives attacks, and eventually returns ill.

l: Yamato-take's death, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take dies after becoming gravely ill during his return journey. His Empresses and children build an august mausoleum and perform songs at his interment.

l: Yamato-take's transformation into a white bird, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: After his death, Yamato-take turns into a white dotterel and flies away. His family pursues the bird, builds mausoleums, and records songs associated with the interment.

l: genealogies of Emperor Kei-Kō, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The unit records the wives, children, and descendants of the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, including the lines leading to several rulers and territorial ancestors.

l: descendants of Yamato-take, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take has six august children, including His Augustness Tarashi-naka-tsu-hiko, King Waka-take, King Ine-yori-wake, King Take-kahiko, King Ashi-kagami-wake, and King Okinaga-ta-wake. The unit traces subsequent descendants through King Kuhi-mata-naga-hiko and later generations.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. XCIV.—Emperor Sei-Mu.
s: Emperor Sei-Mu, identified in the text as the Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko, dwelt at the palace of Taka-anaho at Shiga in Chika-tsu-Afumi and ruled the empire. He wedded Lady Oho-takara and begot King Wata-nuke. He raised Take-uchi to be Prince Minister and established the rulers, boundaries, and departmental lords of the countries. His august years were ninety-five, and his mausoleum was at Tatanami near Saki.

l: Emperor Sei-Mu, Kojiki, Sect. XCIV.—Emperor Sei-Mu.
s: Emperor Sei-Mu, identified as the Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko, dwelt at the palace of Taka-anaho at Shiga in Chika-tsu-Afumi and ruled the empire. He wedded Lady Oho-takara, begot King Wata-nuke, raised Take-uchi to be Prince Minister, and established rulers, boundaries, and departmental lords. He lived ninety-five years, and his mausoleum was at Tatanami near Saki.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. XCIV.—Emperor Sei-Mu.
s: The empire was ruled by the Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko from the palace of Taka-anaho at Shiga in Chika-tsu-Afumi.

l: Lady Oho-takara, Kojiki, Sect. XCIV.—Emperor Sei-Mu.
s: Lady Oho-takara was the daughter of Take-oshiyama-tari-ne, ancestor of the Grandees of Hodzumi. She wedded the Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko and begot King Wata-nuke.

l: King Wata-nuke, Kojiki, Sect. XCIV.—Emperor Sei-Mu.
s: King Wata-nuke was the august child begotten by the Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko and Lady Oho-takara.

l: the Noble Take-uchi, Kojiki, Sect. XCIV.—Emperor Sei-Mu.
s: Take-uchi was raised by the Heavenly Sovereign to the office of Prince Minister.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: This unit concerns Emperor Chiū-Ai, Empress Jin-Gō, their Heir Apparent, and the events surrounding the promised conquest of Korea. Empress Jin-Gō receives divine instructions, leads the crossing to Korea, secures the submission of Shiragi and Kudara, and later subdues Yamato. King Kagosaka dies while seeking an omen, and King Oshikuma dies after opposing the Empress's forces. The Heir Apparent exchanges names with Great Deity Izasa-wake, receives great august liquor, and Emperor Chiū-Ai and Empress Jin-Gō are recorded as dead and buried.

l: Emperor Chiū-Ai, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Emperor Chiū-Ai dwells at the palaces of Toyora and Kashihi and rules the Empire. He fathers King Kagosaka, King Oshikuma, Homu-ya-wake, and Oho-tomo-wake, and dies after refusing to heed the divine promise concerning Korea.

l: Tsukushi, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Tsukushi contains the palace of Kashihi, where Emperor Chiū-Ai dwells, and the Land of Tsukushi, where Empress Jin-Gō returns and gives birth to the august child.

l: King Kagosaka, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: King Kagosaka is a son of Emperor Chiū-Ai. While seeking an omen at the moor of Toga, he climbs an oak-tree and is devoured when a large boar overturns it.

l: King Oshikuma, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: King Oshikuma is a son of Emperor Chiū-Ai and opposes Empress Jin-Gō on her return to Yamato. Pursued after his army is defeated, he and Noble Isahi plunge into the sea and die together.

l: Her Augustness Princess Okinaga-tarashi, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Empress Jin-Gō is divinely possessed and receives instructions promising Korea to the child in her womb. She crosses to Korea, secures the submission of Shiragi and Kudara, subdues Yamato, gives birth to the august child in Tsukushi, and later dies at the age of one hundred.

l: Oho-tomo-wake, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Oho-tomo-wake is a child of Emperor Chiū-Ai and Empress Jin-Gō. He is also called Homuda-wake, and his birth is associated with an arm protuberance resembling an elbow-pad and the prediction that he will rule countries.

l: Emperor Ō-Jin, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Homuda-wake is another name for Oho-tomo-wake, the Heir Apparent whose future rule of countries is foreknown while he is in the womb.

l: Heir Apparent, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The Heir Apparent is the child of Empress Jin-Gō and is placed in a mourning-vessel during the journey to Yamato. He later travels with Noble Take-uchi, exchanges names with Great Deity Izasa-wake, and receives great august liquor.

l: Land of Kumaso, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The Land of Kumaso is the country Emperor Chiū-Ai is preparing to smite when the divine possession of Empress Jin-Gō reveals the promised land to the west.

l: the Noble Take-uchi, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Noble Take-uchi requests the Deities' commands, receives instructions concerning the conquest of Korea, and helps carry out the preparations. He later travels with the Heir Apparent and speaks and sings on the Heir Apparent's behalf.

l: august vessels, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The august vessels cross the great sea after the prescribed offerings and preparations are made. The fishes of the sea-plain carry them on their backs, and a strong favourable wind drives them toward Korea.

l: Land of Shiragi, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The Land of Shiragi is reached and submits to Empress Jin-Gō's authority. It is constituted the feeder of the august horses, and its chieftain promises yearly service and provisions.

l: Land of Kudara, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The Land of Kudara is constituted the crossing store after Empress Jin-Gō secures the submission of the countries reached during the Korean expedition.

l: mourning-vessel, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The mourning-vessel carries the august child while Empress Jin-Gō returns toward Yamato. A report is spread that the child is dead, causing King Oshikuma to mistake the vessel for an empty one.

l: Noble Isahi, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Noble Isahi is made generalissimo by King Oshikuma during the conflict with Empress Jin-Gō's forces. He is pursued with King Oshikuma and dies with him after plunging into the sea.

l: Naniha-ne-ko-take-furu-kuma, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Naniha-ne-ko-take-furu-kuma is made generalissimo on the side of the Heir Apparent. He deceives King Oshikuma's forces by feigning submission, then restores the army's bows and leads the pursuit and defeat of the opposing army.

l: Tsunuga, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Tsunuga is the site of the temporary palace built for the Heir Apparent at the mouth of the Road of Koshi. It is also the name later given to the strand where the blood of the dolphin-fishes stinks.

l: Great Deity Izasa-wake, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Great Deity Izasa-wake appears in a dream and requests an exchange of names with the Heir Apparent. After the exchange, the Heir Apparent receives dolphin-fishes as august food, and the Deity is honoured as the Food-Wondrous-Great-Deity.

l: great august liquor, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The great august liquor is distilled by Empress Jin-Gō and presented to the Heir Apparent. Empress Jin-Gō and Noble Take-uchi sing drinking songs while it is presented and praised.

l: possession of Korea divinely promised, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The possession of Korea divinely promised is announced through the divinely possessed Empress Jin-Gō. The Deities declare that the land is to be ruled by the august child in her womb and prescribe offerings, vessels, and other preparations for crossing the sea.

l: preparations for the conquest of Korea, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The preparations for the conquest of Korea include purification, offerings to Heavenly, Earthly, mountain, river, and sea Deities, placing august spirits on the vessel, preparing ashes, chopsticks, and leaf platters, and equipping and marshalling an army.

l: Empress Jin-Gō conquers Korea, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Empress Jin-Gō conquers Korea by reaching Shiragi, securing its chieftain's submission, and establishing Shiragi as feeder of the august horses and Kudara as the crossing store. She appoints guardian Deities and crosses back to Tsukushi.

l: Empress Jin-Gō subdues Yamato, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Empress Jin-Gō subdues Yamato while concealing the survival of the august child in a mourning-vessel. Her forces defeat King Oshikuma's army at Sasanami, and King Oshikuma and Noble Isahi die in the sea.

l: Yamato, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Yamato is the destination of Empress Jin-Gō's return after the Korean expedition. Because she doubts the disposition of its people, she uses a mourning-vessel and a false report of the child's death before defeating the opposing forces.

l: Heir Apparent exchanges names with the Great Deity Izasa-Wake, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: The Heir Apparent exchanges names with Great Deity Izasa-wake at Tsunuga after the Deity appears in a dream. The exchange is followed by the presentation of dolphin-fishes as august food and the Heir Apparent's new association with the Food-Wondrous-Great-Deity.

l: death of Emperor Chiū-Ai and Empress Jin-Gō, Kojiki, Sect. XCV.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CIII.—Emperor Chiū-Ai (Part IX.—His Death and That of the Empress Jin-Gō).
s: Emperor Chiū-Ai dies after the Deities become angry when he rejects their message, and his august years are given as fifty-two. Empress Jin-Gō later dies at the august age of one hundred; Emperor Chiū-Ai is buried at Nagaye near Wega in Kafuchi, and she is buried at Tatanami in Saki.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: This unit concerns Emperor Ō-Jin, his genealogies, reign, succession arrangements, foreign contacts, and burial. His Augustness Oho-yama-mori, His Augustness Oho-sazaki, and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko receive roles in governing the mountains, sea, Empire, and succession, but conflict follows Emperor Ō-Jin’s death. Ama-no-hi-boko crosses to Japan, and his descendants and eight precious treasures are described. Emperor Ō-Jin is said to have lived 130 years and was buried on the mound of Mofusu at Wega in Kafuchi.

l: Emperor Ō-Jin, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Emperor Ō-Jin, also called His Augustness Homuda-wake or Heavenly Sovereign Homuda, ruled the Empire from the palace of Akira at Karushima. He had twenty-six august children, and the unit recounts his marriages, descendants, deeds, succession arrangements, death, age, and burial.

l: His Augustness Oho-yama-mori, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Oho-yama-mori was assigned to administer the government of the mountains and the sea. After Emperor Ō-Jin’s death, he prepared to attack Uji-no-waki-iratsuko in an attempt to obtain the Empire, but was drowned at Kawara Point and buried on the Nara mountain.

l: His Augustness Oho-sazaki, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Oho-sazaki was assigned to take and deign to report on the government of the realm. After Emperor Ō-Jin’s death, he warned Uji-no-waki-iratsuko of Oho-yama-mori’s attack, later ceded the Empire to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, and ultimately ruled the Empire after Uji-no-waki-iratsuko died.

l: Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Uji-no-waki-iratsuko was designated to rule the succession of Heaven’s sun. After Emperor Ō-Jin’s death, he defeated the attack of His Augustness Oho-yama-mori, and he and His Augustness Oho-sazaki repeatedly ceded the Empire to each other until he died early.

l: Uji, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Uji is the place whose moor the Heavenly Sovereign gazed upon after crossing into Afumi. Uji also appears in the name Uji-no-waki-iratsuko and in the song referring to the Uji ferry and its river-bank.

l: Mofusu at Wega in Kafuchi, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Mofusu at Wega in Kafuchi is the mound where Emperor Ō-Jin’s august mausoleum is located.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The Empire was ruled by Emperor Ō-Jin. His Augustness Oho-yama-mori, His Augustness Oho-sazaki, and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko were assigned or considered in relation to its government and succession.

l: the succession, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The succession was assigned by Emperor Ō-Jin to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, while His Augustness Oho-yama-mori was assigned the mountains and sea and His Augustness Oho-sazaki the government of the realm. After Emperor Ō-Jin’s death, Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko repeatedly ceded the Empire to each other until Uji-no-waki-iratsuko died.

l: the eight precious treasures of Ama-no-hi-boko, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The eight precious treasures of Ama-no-hi-boko were two strings of pearls, a wave-shaking scarf, a wave-cutting scarf, a wind-shaking scarf, a wind-cutting scarf, a mirror of the offing, and a mirror of the shore. They were called the Eight Great Deities of Idzushi.

l: Ama-no-hi-boko, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Ama-no-hi-boko was the child of the ruler of Shiragi and crossed over to Japan. After pursuing his wife to Japan, he landed in the country of Tajima, where he married Saki-tsu-mi and became an ancestor of the descendants described in the unit.

l: Emperor Ō-Jin's reign, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: During Emperor Ō-Jin’s reign, the Fisher Tribe, Mountain Tribe, Mountain Warden Tribe, and Ise Tribe were established, the Pool of Tsurugi and Pool of Kudara were made, and people and tribute came from Shiragi and Kudara.

l: the death of Emperor Ō-Jin, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: After the death of Emperor Ō-Jin, His Augustness Oho-sazaki followed the Heavenly Sovereign’s commands and ceded the Empire to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko. The death was followed by Oho-yama-mori’s attempted attack and the later mutual ceding of the Empire by Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko.

l: the succession conflict, Kojiki, Sect. CIV.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part 1.—Genealogies). .. Sect. CXVIII.—Emperor Ō-Jin (Part XV.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The succession conflict arose after Emperor Ō-Jin’s death when His Augustness Oho-yama-mori sought to obtain the Empire despite the command assigning succession to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko. Oho-yama-mori attacked but was drowned, after which Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko continued to cede the Empire to each other.
